overview: A quantum computer is a physical machine. Its qubits are real physical systems — for example tiny superconducting circuits, individual trapped ions, neutral atoms held by lasers, or particles of light — that are controlled and measured with electronics, lasers or microwaves. Running a circuit on it means physically manipulating those qubits and then reading out classical results. Real devices are noisy, and each run produces just one set of measurement outcomes (a shot).

A quantum simulator (in this course: a quantum circuit simulator) is ordinary software running on an ordinary classical computer. It calculates, using linear algebra, what a quantum circuit would do. The most common type, the state-vector simulator, stores all 2ⁿ amplitudes of an n-qubit state, updates them gate by gate, and then either reports the exact probabilities or samples simulated shots from them. Nothing quantum is physically happening inside the simulator.

Simulators are indispensable for learning, designing and debugging circuits because they are cheap, fast for small circuits, noise-free (if you want them to be), and let you look inside the computation. But the cost of storing a general state doubles with every extra qubit, so simulators run out of memory at a few dozen qubits. That growth is exactly why real quantum computers are interesting (Topics 1.2–1.3) — and why simulators eventually stop being able to stand in for them.

Why the learner needs this: nearly everything the learner will do in this course — running circuits, checking results, doing labs — happens on a simulator. Knowing what the simulator is, and is not, prevents false conclusions such as "my circuit will behave this way on a real device" or "the simulator proves quantum computers are unnecessary".
Where it fits: this topic closes the "big picture" unit by moving from what quantum computers can do (1.2–1.3) to how we actually work with them (simulators and hardware).

Connection to Topics 1.2–1.3: the 2ⁿ amplitude count from Topic 1.2 is precisely what limits simulators; the noise and "advantage" discussion in Topic 1.3 explains why hardware results differ and why classical simulation methods are used to test advantage claims.
After this topic the learner can: predict simulator memory needs, read counts versus probabilities correctly, explain unexpected hardware results, and choose the right tool for a task.
• n qubits are described by 2ⁿ complex amplitudes; measuring returns only n classical bits.
• Measurement probabilities come from squared amplitude magnitudes: P(x) = |c_x|².
• Quantum gates are reversible (unitary) transformations of the amplitudes.
• Current quantum devices are noisy; a single run is random, so circuits are run many times (shots).
• Quantum advantage means beating the best classical methods — which include classical simulation.

mathematical_foundations: 6. Mathematical Foundations
EQUATION: |ψ_after⟩ = U_m ⋯ U_2 U_1 |ψ_0⟩
NAME: Circuit evolution (what a simulator computes)
MEANING: The final state is the initial state multiplied by each gate's matrix in order.
VARIABLES: |ψ_0⟩ = initial state (usually |00…0⟩); U_k = matrix of gate k; m = number of gates.
WHY IT MATTERS: This is exactly the calculation a state-vector simulator performs.
BEGINNER INTERPRETATION: Apply the gates one after the other to the list of amplitudes.
EXAMPLE: E02.
EQUATION: Memory ≈ 2ⁿ × 16 bytes
NAME: State-vector memory
MEANING: Memory needed to store an n-qubit double-precision complex state.
VARIABLES: n = number of qubits; 16 bytes = one complex amplitude (two 8-byte floats).
WHY IT MATTERS: Explains the qubit limit of state-vector simulators.
BEGINNER INTERPRETATION: One more qubit means twice as much memory.
EXAMPLE: n = 30 → 16 GiB (E01).
EQUATION: P(x) = |c_x|²
NAME: Born rule (as used in simulators)
MEANING: Probability of outcome x from its amplitude c_x.
VARIABLES: c_x = amplitude of basis state x.
WHY IT MATTERS: Simulators use it both to report exact probabilities and to draw shots.
BEGINNER INTERPRETATION: Square the amplitude's size.
EQUATION: standard error = √(p(1−p)/N)
NAME: Shot-noise (binomial) standard error
MEANING: Typical size of the random error in a measured frequency.
VARIABLES: p = true outcome probability; N = number of shots.
WHY IT MATTERS: Tells learners how many shots they need and how much variation is normal.
BEGINNER INTERPRETATION: More shots help, but only slowly.
EQUATION: Memory (density matrix) ≈ 4ⁿ × 16 bytes
NAME: Density-matrix memory
MEANING: Storing a 2ⁿ × 2ⁿ complex matrix.
VARIABLES: n = number of qubits.
WHY IT MATTERS: Shows why noisy exact simulation reaches fewer qubits than the state-vector method.
BEGINNER INTERPRETATION: Each added qubit multiplies memory by four.
EXAMPLE: n = 15 → 4¹⁵ × 16 bytes = 2³⁰ × 16 = 16 GiB (equivalent to a 30-qubit state vector).
EQUATION: Clifford gates = {H, S, CNOT, …}; Clifford circuits are classically simulable in polynomial time (Gottesman–Knill)
NAME: Gottesman–Knill theorem (informal statement)
MEANING: Circuits that start in computational-basis states, use only Clifford gates and end with computational-basis measurements can be simulated efficiently on a classical computer.
VARIABLES: None.
WHY IT MATTERS: Shows that entanglement alone does not make a circuit hard to simulate.
BEGINNER INTERPRETATION: Some very entangled circuits are still easy for a classical computer.
EXAMPLE: A 40-qubit GHZ circuit (E04).

DEFINITION: An error where the measured value of a qubit differs from its actual state.

activities: 10. Hands-On Activities
ACTIVITY ID: A01
TITLE: Inside the Bell circuit, and which "simulator" is which
OBJECTIVE: See the state vector at each step and separate the three meanings of "simulator".
STARTING STATE: Two qubits in |00⟩, ideal state-vector simulator with "show state vector" enabled.
STEPS:
1. Apply H to q0 and read the amplitudes.
2. Apply CNOT (control q0, target q1) and read the amplitudes and probabilities.
3. Sort these phrases into the three meanings (V07): "a laptop program running my circuit", "estimating a molecule's energy", "cold atoms in a laser lattice imitating a magnet".
4. Try to find the "show amplitudes" option for a real-device run.

EXPECTED OBSERVATION: After H: amplitudes ≈ (0.707, 0, 0.707, 0) in order 00, 01, 10, 11. After CNOT: (0.707, 0, 0, 0.707); probabilities 0.5 / 0 / 0 / 0.5. Phrase sorting: circuit simulator, quantum simulation (task), analog simulator. No amplitude view exists for hardware.
WHY THIS HAPPENS: The simulator stores the full state; hardware reveals only measurement outcomes.
TRY THIS: Swap the gate order (CNOT first, then H) and compare.
EXPECTED RESULT: CNOT first leaves |00⟩ unchanged; then H gives (|00⟩ + |10⟩)/√2: P(00) = P(10) = 0.5.
OPEN QUESTION: Why can a simulator show amplitudes but a device cannot?
ACTIVITY ID: A02
TITLE: Shots and statistical noise
OBJECTIVE: Observe how counts converge to probabilities.
STARTING STATE: Bell circuit on an ideal simulator in sampling mode.
STEPS:
1. Run with 10, 100, 1,000 and 10,000 shots, three times each.
2. Record the count of 00 each time.
3. Compare the spread with ±√(p(1−p)/N).
EXPECTED OBSERVATION: Counts vary from run to run; spread is wide for 10 shots and narrow for 10,000; 01 and 10 never appear in the ideal simulation.
WHY THIS HAPPENS: Each shot is an independent random sample; relative fluctuations shrink as 1/√N.
TRY THIS: Fix the random seed and repeat to see identical results.
EXPECTED RESULT: Expected fraction of 00 ≈ 0.5 with standard error 0.158 (N=10), 0.05 (N=100), 0.0158 (N=1,000), 0.005 (N=10,000).
OPEN QUESTION: How many shots would you need to halve the error of the N = 1,000 estimate? (Answer direction: about four times as many.)
ACTIVITY ID: A03
TITLE: Ideal vs noisy
OBJECTIVE: See how noise changes a Bell-state result.
STARTING STATE: Bell circuit, 4,000 shots, noise slider at zero.
STEPS:
1. Run on the ideal simulator and note the counts.
2. Switch on a simple noise model (readout error, then gate error) and increase noise gradually.
3. Record when 01 and 10 appear and by how much 00 and 11 fall.
EXPECTED OBSERVATION: With zero noise, 01 and 10 never appear; with noise they appear and grow as the noise level increases.
WHY THIS HAPPENS: Errors move probability into outcomes the ideal circuit forbids.
TRY THIS: Add a longer chain of gates and observe larger deviations.
EXPECTED RESULT: Ideal: 00 ≈ 50%, 11 ≈ 50%, 01 = 10 = 0%. Noisy: 01 and 10 > 0 (exact amounts depend on the chosen model).
OPEN QUESTION: Would you conclude the circuit is wrong if 01 and 10 each appear in about 1–2% of shots? What more would you check?
ACTIVITY ID: A04
TITLE: Where do simulators run out?
OBJECTIVE: Find the practical limits and see how stabilizer simulation escapes them.
STARTING STATE: Memory slider (V03), laptop memory set to 16 GiB.
STEPS:
1. Find the largest n whose state vector fits in 16 GiB.
2. Build GHZ circuits of 5, 10, 20 and 40 qubits (H on q0, then CNOT from each qubit to the next) and run them with a state-vector simulator, then with a stabilizer simulator.
3. Compare run times and which sizes succeed.
EXPECTED OBSERVATION: The state-vector method fails or becomes impractical beyond about 30 qubits on 16 GiB; the stabilizer simulator handles all sizes quickly.
WHY THIS HAPPENS: State-vector memory ∝ 2ⁿ; GHZ circuits are Clifford, so a stabilizer simulator avoids storing 2ⁿ amplitudes.
TRY THIS: Add a single T gate and observe what happens in the stabilizer simulator.
EXPECTED RESULT: Largest n for 16 GiB at 16 bytes/amplitude: 2ⁿ × 16 ≤ 2³⁴ → n ≤ 30. GHZ results (ideal): all-zeros ≈ 50%, all-ones ≈ 50%, all other outcomes 0%.
OPEN QUESTION: If Clifford circuits are easy, which gate would you add to make a circuit hard again?

TOPIC 1.4 — QUANTUM COMPUTERS VS QUANTUM SIMULATORS

Source material for the QuantumLearnAI knowledge pack. Same structure and notation as Topics 1.2 and 1.3. Conventions: kets are written |0⟩, |1⟩; multi-qubit labels are written q0 q1 (leftmost = q0). Qiskit-style tools print the reverse order (q1 q0), so the tutor must always state which ordering it uses. Why this topic matters for the project: QuantumLearnAI treats the simulator as the authority for ideal circuit results (Topic 1.2, Section 14). This topic explains what a simulator is, what it can and cannot tell the learner, and how its results differ from those of real hardware. That is a project convention as well as a scientific point: a simulator is authoritative for what an ideal circuit does, not for what a physical device will output. Verification note: numerical and circuit results were derived by hand; confirm in the project simulator before release. This topic contains no vendor-specific numbers (qubit counts, error rates, prices), because those change quickly and are out of scope. Syllabus assumption: Topics 1.2–1.3 introduced qubits, superposition, interference, entanglement, measurement, 2ⁿ amplitudes, shots-based thinking, noisy (NISQ) devices and the meaning of "quantum advantage". 1. Topic Metadata
TOPIC ID:
TOPIC TITLE:
Quantum Computers vs Quantum Simulators
CATEGORY:
Quantum Computing Fundamentals
DIFFICULTY:
Beginner
ESTIMATED LEARNING TIME:
30–40 minutes
PREREQUISITES:

SHORT DESCRIPTION:

This topic explains the difference between a real quantum computer (a physical device) and a quantum simulator (a classical program that calculates what a quantum circuit would do). Learners see how a simulator works, why its cost doubles with every added qubit, what a simulator can show that hardware cannot, why hardware results differ from ideal results, and when each tool should be used.
LEARNING OBJECTIVES:
By the end of this topic, the learner should be able to:
1. Explain the difference between a quantum computer and a quantum simulator, including what hardware each runs on.
2. Describe how a state-vector simulator applies gates and produces measurement probabilities, and carry out a two-qubit example by hand.
3. Calculate the memory needed to store an n-qubit state vector and explain why simulation does not scale to large general circuits.
4. Distinguish exact probabilities from sampled shot counts, and estimate the statistical uncertainty of a shot-based estimate.
5. List at least three reasons why a circuit's results on real hardware can differ from its ideal simulation.

6. Identify circuit families that can be simulated efficiently on a classical computer (Clifford circuits, low entanglement) and explain why this does not contradict the difficulty of general simulation.
7. Decide whether a simulator or real hardware is the right tool for a given task, and avoid confusing "quantum simulator" with "quantum simulation" of physical systems.
2. Topic Overview
2.1 What is this topic?

A quantum computer is a physical machine. Its qubits are real physical systems — for example tiny superconducting circuits, individual trapped ions, neutral atoms held by lasers, or particles of light — that are controlled and measured with electronics, lasers or microwaves. Running a circuit on it means physically manipulating those qubits and then reading out classical results. Real devices are noisy, and each run produces just one set of measurement outcomes (a shot).

A quantum simulator (in this course: a quantum circuit simulator) is ordinary software running on an ordinary classical computer. It calculates, using linear algebra, what a quantum circuit would do. The most common type, the state-vector simulator, stores all 2ⁿ amplitudes of an n-qubit state, updates them gate by gate, and then either reports the exact probabilities or samples simulated shots from them. Nothing quantum is physically happening inside the simulator.

Simulators are indispensable for learning, designing and debugging circuits because they are cheap, fast for small circuits, noise-free (if you want them to be), and let you look inside the computation. But the cost of storing a general state doubles with every extra qubit, so simulators run out of memory at a few dozen qubits. That growth is exactly why real quantum computers are interesting (Topics 1.2–1.3) — and why simulators eventually stop being able to stand in for them.
2.2 Why does it matter?

Why the learner needs this: nearly everything the learner will do in this course — running circuits, checking results, doing labs — happens on a simulator. Knowing what the simulator is, and is not, prevents false conclusions such as "my circuit will behave this way on a real device" or "the simulator proves quantum computers are unnecessary".
Where it fits: this topic closes the "big picture" unit by moving from what quantum computers can do (1.2–1.3) to how we actually work with them (simulators and hardware).

Connection to Topics 1.2–1.3: the 2ⁿ amplitude count from Topic 1.2 is precisely what limits simulators; the noise and "advantage" discussion in Topic 1.3 explains why hardware results differ and why classical simulation methods are used to test advantage claims.
After this topic the learner can: predict simulator memory needs, read counts versus probabilities correctly, explain unexpected hardware results, and choose the right tool for a task.
2.3 Prerequisite recap
Before learning Topic 1.4, remember:
• n qubits are described by 2ⁿ complex amplitudes; measuring returns only n classical bits.
• Measurement probabilities come from squared amplitude magnitudes: P(x) = |c_x|².
• Quantum gates are reversible (unitary) transformations of the amplitudes.
• Current quantum devices are noisy; a single run is random, so circuits are run many times (shots).
• Quantum advantage means beating the best classical methods — which include classical simulation.
3. Concepts
CONCEPT 1
Concept ID:
Concept Title:
What a Real Quantum Computer Is
What is it?

A physical device whose qubits are real quantum systems, controlled by hardware (microwave pulses, lasers, magnetic fields, optics) and read out by measurement electronics. Its result for each run is a string of classical bits.
Why does it matter?
Only hardware can run quantum circuits "natively" and, once large and reliable enough, offer speedups that classical simulation cannot match.
How does it work?

A circuit is translated ("compiled") into the device's native gates and qubit connections, executed by physically acting on the qubits, and then measured. Each execution gives one outcome string; repeating many times (shots) builds up a histogram. Several physical platforms exist (for example superconducting circuits, trapped ions, neutral atoms, photonic systems, spin systems in semiconductors); they differ in speed, connectivity and error behaviour, and the landscape changes quickly.
Visual explanation:
A pipeline: circuit → compile to native gates → control electronics/lasers → qubits → measurement → bit-string. A label shows "one random outcome per shot; noise present".
Technical explanation:
Hardware qubits suffer decoherence and gate/readout errors; the executed operation is only an approximation of the ideal unitary circuit.
Mathematical representation:
None required (conceptual).
Example:
Running the Bell-state circuit on hardware 1000 times yields counts mostly at 00 and 11, plus a small number of 01 and 10 outcomes caused by errors.
Common mistake:
Imagining a quantum computer returns exact probabilities or amplitudes. It returns only sampled bit-strings.
Connection to previous concepts:
Applies Topic 1.2 (measurement gives one outcome) and Topic 1.3 (NISQ devices are noisy).
Try it:
Compare an "ideal" and a "hardware-style noisy" result for the same circuit (Activity A03).
Key takeaway:
A quantum computer is a physical machine that produces noisy, sampled classical outputs from real qubits.
CONCEPT 2
Concept ID:
Concept Title:
What a Quantum Simulator Is (and the Terminology Trap)
What is it?
A quantum circuit simulator is classical software that computes the effect of quantum circuits mathematically. The word "simulator" is overloaded, so three different things must be kept apart:
• Quantum circuit simulator — classical software mimicking a quantum circuit (the subject of this topic).
• Quantum simulation (of physical systems) — the *task* of modelling molecules or materials (Topic 1.3, C04), which can be attempted on a quantum computer.
• Analog quantum simulator — a purpose-built physical quantum system (such as cold atoms in a lattice) engineered to mimic another quantum system. It is real quantum hardware, not a program.
Why does it matter?
Misreading these terms leads to confusion such as "a quantum simulator is a quantum computer" or "quantum simulation can be done on my laptop simulator at any size".
How does it work?
A circuit simulator represents the quantum state as numbers in memory and applies each gate as a matrix operation. Different simulator designs exist (C03, C07).
Visual explanation:
A Venn-style diagram with three labelled circles — "circuit simulator (software)", "quantum simulation (the task)", "analog quantum simulator (special hardware)" — with short examples in each.
Technical explanation:
Circuit simulators are deterministic classical programs; any randomness in their output comes from a pseudo-random number generator used for sampling shots.
Mathematical representation:
|ψ_after⟩ = U_m ⋯ U_2 U_1 |ψ_0⟩   (the simulator multiplies the state by each gate's matrix in turn)
Example:
"Run my circuit on the simulator" means run it on a classical program; "simulate a molecule" means the physics task; "analog simulator" refers to a lab experiment.
Common mistake:
Treating the three meanings as one.
Connection to previous concepts:
Refers back to Topic 1.3 C04 (simulating quantum systems).
Try it:
Sort example sentences into the three meanings (Activity A01, part 3).
Key takeaway:
In this course, "quantum simulator" means classical software that computes what a quantum circuit does; it is not quantum hardware.
CONCEPT 3
Concept ID:
Concept Title:
State-Vector Simulation and Why It Doesn't Scale
What is it?
A state-vector simulator stores all 2ⁿ amplitudes of the n-qubit state and updates them for each gate.
Why does it matter?
It is the standard, most transparent simulator: it is exact (up to rounding), gives full access to amplitudes, and mirrors the maths taught in this course. Its limit is memory and time.
How does it work?

Start with |00…0⟩ (amplitude 1 for the all-zero string, 0 elsewhere). For each gate, multiply the affected parts of the vector by the gate's matrix. A single-qubit gate updates pairs of amplitudes; a two-qubit gate updates groups of four. Each gate touches essentially all 2ⁿ amplitudes, so work per gate also grows like 2ⁿ. At the end, probabilities are |amplitude|²; shots are drawn from those probabilities.
Memory: with one 128-bit complex number (two 64-bit floats) per amplitude, the state needs 2ⁿ × 16 bytes. Adding one qubit doubles memory and time per gate.
Visual explanation:
A vector with 2ⁿ rows that grows as n increases; side panel showing "memory needed" with a slider for n, and a marker for the memory of a typical laptop.
Technical explanation:
Single-precision (8 bytes per amplitude) halves the memory but reduces accuracy; some simulators trade precision for size.
Mathematical representation:
Memory ≈ 2ⁿ × 16 bytes (double-precision complex);  amplitudes = 2ⁿ.
Example:
See E01 (memory table) and E02 (a two-qubit Bell circuit done by hand).
Common mistake:
Assuming a simulator can handle "as many qubits as you like". General circuits with more than roughly 30–40 qubits exceed ordinary memory, and about 50 qubits need petabyte-scale memory.
Connection to previous concepts:
Directly applies Topic 1.2 C06 (exponential state space).
Try it:
Increase n in the memory slider and note where your own machine's memory would run out (Activity A04).
Key takeaway:
A state-vector simulator is exact but needs 2ⁿ amplitudes, so its cost doubles with every added qubit.
CONCEPT 4
Concept ID:
Concept Title:
Exact Probabilities vs Sampled Shots
What is it?

A simulator can report the *exact* probability of every outcome from the state vector. Both simulators and real hardware can also produce *shots*: individual random outcomes that, collected together, give counts that only approximate the probabilities.
Why does it matter?
Learners often compare "exact" results with "counts" and are confused by differences. Counts fluctuate randomly; the fluctuations shrink slowly as the number of shots grows.
How does it work?

If an outcome has probability p, then in N shots its measured frequency has standard error √(p(1−p)/N). With more shots the estimate improves, but only as 1/√N — 100 times more shots gives only 10 times smaller error. Real hardware gives only counts; an ideal state-vector simulator can give both.
Visual explanation:
Side-by-side bars: exact probabilities (e.g. 50%/50%) and a histogram of counts that wobbles around them; a slider for number of shots shows the histogram converging.
Technical explanation:
Shot outcomes are independent random samples from the Born-rule distribution P(x) = |c_x|².
Mathematical representation:
standard error = √(p(1−p)/N)
Example:
See E03: for N = 1,000 shots of a 50/50 outcome, expect about 500 ± 16 (one standard error), and roughly 468–532 for about 95% of runs.
Common mistake:
Expecting exactly 500/500 from 1000 shots, or treating a 490/510 split as evidence that the circuit is wrong.
Connection to previous concepts:
Extends Topic 1.2 C03 (measurement is probabilistic; repeat to see probabilities).
Try it:
Run the same circuit with 10, 100, 1,000 and 10,000 shots (Activity A02).
Key takeaway:
A simulator can show exact probabilities; hardware and sampled simulation give counts that fluctuate around them, shrinking only as 1/√N.
CONCEPT 5
Concept ID:
Concept Title:
What a Simulator Can Show That Hardware Cannot
What is it?

Because a state-vector simulator holds the full state in memory, it can display things no physical device can reveal: the complete set of amplitudes (including phases), the state after each gate, and exact probabilities without sampling.
Why does it matter?

This is a powerful teaching and debugging feature, and it is also why simulator output must not be confused with something a real machine could give you. It explains why a result is "visible" in a lab but "unreadable" on hardware (Topic 1.2, M07).
How does it work?

A simulator can "save the state vector" at any step. On hardware, measurement is the only way to extract information, and it destroys the superposition; reading out all amplitudes would require preparing the same state very many times and using specialised techniques (state tomography), whose cost grows exponentially with qubit number.
Visual explanation:

A circuit with a "peek inside" marker after each gate in simulator mode, showing amplitude bars (with sign/phase arrows); on the hardware side the same marker is greyed out with the label "not available".
Technical explanation:
Looking inside is a simulator-only feature, so it breaks the rules that apply on real devices.
Mathematical representation:
Simulator output after gate k: |ψ_k⟩ = U_k ⋯ U_1 |ψ_0⟩ (all amplitudes visible).
Example:
After H on |0⟩ the simulator can show amplitudes (0.707, 0.707); hardware can only return many 0s and 1s that approximate 50/50.
Common mistake:
Designing an algorithm that "reads the amplitudes" at the end — fine in a simulator, impossible on hardware.
Connection to previous concepts:
Reinforces Topic 1.2 M07: n qubits have 2ⁿ amplitudes but measurement returns only n bits.
Try it:
Step through the Bell circuit and see the amplitudes after each gate (Activity A01).
Key takeaway:
A simulator lets you look inside the computation; a quantum computer only gives you measurement outcomes.
CONCEPT 6
Concept ID:
Concept Title:
Why Hardware Results Differ from Ideal Simulation
What is it?
Physical devices introduce imperfections that a noise-free simulator does not model, so results differ from the ideal predictions.
Why does it matter?
When a hardware result looks "wrong", it is usually not a bug in the learner's circuit but a sign of noise or hardware constraints. Learners need to know the main causes.
How does it work?
Common sources of difference:
• **Gate errors:** operations are slightly imperfect.
• **Readout errors:** a qubit measured as 0 may be reported as 1 or vice versa.
• **Decoherence:** qubits lose their quantum state over time; longer circuits suffer more.
• **Crosstalk:** operations on one qubit disturb neighbours.
• **Limited connectivity and native gate set:** not every pair of qubits can interact directly, so the circuit is compiled with extra operations (such as swaps), making it longer and noisier.
• **Finite shots:** statistical fluctuation, present even with perfect hardware.
Simulators can include a **noise model** — a mathematical approximation of such errors — to give a more realistic prediction, but it is only a model.
Visual explanation:
An ideal Bell-state histogram (only 00 and 11) beside a noisy one with small bars at 01 and 10, with callouts naming the likely causes.
Technical explanation:
Noise is described by error channels (for example depolarising or readout-flip channels); simulating these requires either repeated random sampling of errors or a density-matrix representation (C07).
Mathematical representation:
Readout error example (illustrative): if a qubit in |0⟩ is misread as 1 with probability e, measured P(1) = e. For e = 0.02, 2% of shots read 1 even for a perfect |0⟩.
Example:
A Bell-state circuit on hardware: ideal result 00 ≈ 50%, 11 ≈ 50%, 01 = 10 = 0%. On hardware, 01 and 10 appear with small non-zero probability.
Common mistake:
Concluding that the circuit is wrong, or that entanglement "did not work", because a small number of 01/10 outcomes appear.
Connection to previous concepts:
Applies Topic 1.3 C08 (NISQ devices; noise and error correction).
Try it:
Raise the noise level in the noisy simulator and watch 01/10 counts appear (Activity A03).
Key takeaway:
Hardware results differ from ideal ones because of noise, decoherence, readout errors, limited connectivity and finite shots; a noise model only approximates this.
CONCEPT 7
Concept ID:
Concept Title:
Types of Simulators and Circuits That Are Easy to Simulate
What is it?
Different simulation methods trade generality against cost, and some important circuit families can be simulated efficiently on a classical computer.
Why does it matter?

It explains why "has entanglement" does not mean "hard to simulate", why simulators can handle certain large circuits, and how classical simulation methods are used to test quantum-advantage claims (Topic 1.3 C08).
How does it work?
• **State-vector simulator:** stores 2ⁿ amplitudes; exact; cost doubles per qubit.
• **Density-matrix simulator:** stores a 2ⁿ × 2ⁿ matrix, which can represent noisy (mixed) states; memory grows like 4ⁿ, so it reaches fewer qubits.

• **Stabilizer (Clifford) simulator:** simulates circuits made only of Clifford gates (such as H, S and CNOT) with computational-basis input and measurement in time polynomial in n. This is the Gottesman–Knill theorem. These circuits can generate highly entangled states (including Bell and GHZ states) yet remain classically easy. Adding a non-Clifford gate (such as T) breaks this efficiency.
• **Tensor-network / matrix-product-state simulator:** exploits limited entanglement or special structure; efficient when entanglement stays low, expensive when it grows.
Hence classical simulation is hard in general, but easy for special cases. Quantum advantage claims must therefore be compared with the best classical methods, including these ones.
Visual explanation:
A map of four simulator types, each with a "what limits it" label (memory 2ⁿ / memory 4ⁿ / non-Clifford gates / entanglement).
Technical explanation:
Efficiency depends on the structure of the circuit, not only on its qubit count.
Mathematical representation:
State-vector memory ∝ 2ⁿ;  density-matrix memory ∝ 4ⁿ;  stabilizer simulation time ∝ polynomial in n (Clifford circuits).
Example:
A 40-qubit GHZ-state circuit (H on q0, then a chain of CNOTs) can be simulated easily by a stabilizer simulator even though a 40-qubit state vector needs 16 TiB (E04).
Common mistake:
Assuming entanglement alone makes a circuit hard to simulate classically.
Connection to previous concepts:
Builds on Topic 1.2 C07 (entanglement) and Topic 1.3 C08 (advantage claims versus classical baselines).
Try it:
Simulate GHZ states with increasing n using the stabilizer method (Activity A04).
Key takeaway:
General quantum circuits are hard to simulate classically, but structured ones — Clifford circuits or low-entanglement circuits — can be simulated efficiently.
CONCEPT 8
Concept ID:
Concept Title:
Choosing Between a Simulator and a Quantum Computer
What is it?
A practical decision guide for which tool fits which job.
Why does it matter?
Using hardware for tasks a simulator handles wastes time and adds noise; using a simulator for tasks beyond its reach gives wrong expectations.
How does it work?

Use a simulator to: learn concepts; design and debug circuits; check ideal outputs; study the effect of a noise model; and test small algorithms. Use real hardware to: observe real noise and errors; benchmark devices; validate that a circuit works under real constraints; and run circuits beyond simulation reach (when large and reliable enough). Typical workflow: design → test on an ideal simulator → test on a noisy simulator → run on hardware → compare with the ideal prediction. Hardware access is typically via the cloud, with queues and limited availability.
Visual explanation:
A workflow diagram of the five steps with a "fastest/cheapest" to "most realistic" gradient bar.
Technical explanation:
Agreement between simulator and hardware outputs, up to expected noise, is evidence that the circuit was implemented correctly.
Mathematical representation:
None required.
Example:
A learner checks that a 3-qubit circuit produces the expected truth table on a simulator, then runs it on hardware to see how noise changes the counts.
Common mistake:
Believing that "it works on the simulator" guarantees the same output on a real device.
Connection to previous concepts:
Combines C03–C07 into practice.
Try it:
Use the decision cards in Example E04 and Activity A01.
Key takeaway:
Develop and debug on simulators; use hardware to learn about real behaviour and to go beyond what simulators can handle.

5. Worked Examples
EXAMPLE ID: E01
TITLE: How much memory does a state-vector simulator need?
RELATED CONCEPT: C03
GOAL: Compute memory for several qubit counts.
GIVEN: Double-precision complex amplitudes at 16 bytes each.
STEP 1: Amplitudes = 2ⁿ.
STEP 2: Memory = 2ⁿ × 16 bytes = 2^(n+4) bytes.
STEP 3: Convert to binary units (1 KiB = 2¹⁰ bytes, 1 MiB = 2²⁰, 1 GiB = 2³⁰, 1 TiB = 2⁴⁰, 1 PiB = 2⁵⁰).
CALCULATION:
n = 10 → 2¹⁴ bytes = 16 KiB
n = 20 → 2²⁴ bytes = 16 MiB
n = 25 → 2²⁹ bytes = 512 MiB
n = 30 → 2³⁴ bytes = 16 GiB
n = 40 → 2⁴⁴ bytes = 16 TiB
n = 50 → 2⁵⁴ bytes = 16 PiB
RESULT: Memory doubles with each qubit: ordinary machines run out between roughly 30 and 35 qubits for a general circuit.
INTERPRETATION: This is the practical face of Topic 1.2's 2ⁿ amplitudes.
COMMON MISTAKE: Forgetting that each amplitude is a *complex* number needing two floating-point numbers (16 bytes).
TRY YOURSELF: How much memory for n = 32? (Answer: 2³⁶ bytes = 64 GiB.)
EXAMPLE ID: E02
TITLE: Simulating a Bell circuit by hand with a state vector
RELATED CONCEPT: C03, C05
GOAL: Show exactly what a simulator computes.
GIVEN: Two qubits, circuit H on q0, then CNOT (control q0, target q1). Basis order: 00, 01, 10, 11. Initial state |00⟩.
STEP 1: Initial vector = (1, 0, 0, 0).
STEP 2: H on q0 mixes 00 with 10 (the basis states that differ in q0): each gets amplitude 1/√2 → (1/√2, 0, 1/√2, 0).
STEP 3: CNOT flips q1 when q0 = 1, so 10 becomes 11 and 11 would become 10 → (1/√2, 0, 0, 1/√2).
STEP 4: Probabilities = squared magnitudes.
CALCULATION:
RESULT: Exact probabilities: 00 → 50%, 11 → 50%, 01 → 0%, 10 → 0%.
INTERPRETATION: The simulator returns these exact numbers; sampling 1000 shots would give counts near 500 and 500, never exactly guaranteed.
COMMON MISTAKE: Applying CNOT before H (that gives a different result: the state stays |00⟩).
TRY YOURSELF: Repeat the calculation with the initial state |01⟩ (q0 = 0, q1 = 1). (Answer: after H: (|01⟩ + |11⟩)/√2; after CNOT: (|01⟩ + |10⟩)/√2, so P(01) = P(10) = 0.5.)

EXAMPLE ID: E03
TITLE: How far can counts stray from the ideal?
RELATED CONCEPT: C04
GOAL: Quantify shot-noise for 1000 shots.
GIVEN: An outcome with true probability p = 0.5, N = 1000 shots.
STEP 1: Standard error = √(p(1−p)/N).
STEP 2: Compute for p = 0.5, N = 1000.
STEP 3: Convert to counts and a two-standard-error range.
CALCULATION:
Expected count = 500; one standard error in counts ≈ 0.0158 × 1000 ≈ 15.8
Two standard errors ≈ 31.6 → range ≈ 468 to 532 (roughly 95% of runs)
RESULT: Counts such as 487 and 513 are entirely normal for an ideal 50/50 outcome.
INTERPRETATION: Do not judge a circuit by an exact 500/500 split.
COMMON MISTAKE: Treating 487/513 as evidence of a bug.
TRY YOURSELF: What is the standard error of the estimated probability for N = 10,000? (Answer: 0.005.)
EXAMPLE ID: E04
TITLE: Which tool for which job?
RELATED CONCEPT: C07, C08
GOAL: Practise choosing the right simulator or hardware.
GIVEN: Four tasks.
(a) Check that a 3-qubit circuit gives the expected truth table.
(b) Study how noise affects a Bell-state experiment on a real device.
(c) Prepare and measure a 40-qubit GHZ state (H on q0, then a chain of CNOTs).
(d) Run a generic, highly entangled 60-qubit circuit with many T gates and read the exact output distribution.
STEP 1: Estimate memory for a general state-vector simulation of each.
STEP 2: Check whether the circuit is Clifford-only.
STEP 3: Decide.
CALCULATION:
(a) 3 qubits → 8 amplitudes: trivial for a state-vector simulator.
(b) Needs real noise → hardware (or a noise model as an approximation).
(c) 40-qubit state vector = 16 TiB (E01), but the GHZ circuit uses only H and CNOT (Clifford) → stabilizer simulator is efficient.
(d) 60 qubits × general gates (T is non-Clifford) → state vector needs 2⁶⁴ bytes = 16 EiB; no efficient general method applies.

RESULT: (a) ideal state-vector simulator; (b) hardware; (c) stabilizer simulator; (d) beyond practical classical simulation in general — hardware is the only way to run it, though extracting the exact distribution would still be impractical.
INTERPRETATION: The right tool depends on the goal and on the circuit's structure, not just on the qubit count.
COMMON MISTAKE: Assuming (c) needs a quantum computer because "40 qubits is too big to simulate".
TRY YOURSELF: Would a 100-qubit circuit made only of H, S and CNOT be efficiently simulable? (Answer: yes, by a stabilizer simulator.)
6. Mathematical Foundations
EQUATION: |ψ_after⟩ = U_m ⋯ U_2 U_1 |ψ_0⟩
NAME: Circuit evolution (what a simulator computes)
MEANING: The final state is the initial state multiplied by each gate's matrix in order.
VARIABLES: |ψ_0⟩ = initial state (usually |00…0⟩); U_k = matrix of gate k; m = number of gates.
WHY IT MATTERS: This is exactly the calculation a state-vector simulator performs.
BEGINNER INTERPRETATION: Apply the gates one after the other to the list of amplitudes.
EXAMPLE: E02.
EQUATION: Memory ≈ 2ⁿ × 16 bytes
NAME: State-vector memory
MEANING: Memory needed to store an n-qubit double-precision complex state.
VARIABLES: n = number of qubits; 16 bytes = one complex amplitude (two 8-byte floats).
WHY IT MATTERS: Explains the qubit limit of state-vector simulators.
BEGINNER INTERPRETATION: One more qubit means twice as much memory.
EXAMPLE: n = 30 → 16 GiB (E01).
EQUATION: P(x) = |c_x|²
NAME: Born rule (as used in simulators)
MEANING: Probability of outcome x from its amplitude c_x.
VARIABLES: c_x = amplitude of basis state x.
WHY IT MATTERS: Simulators use it both to report exact probabilities and to draw shots.
BEGINNER INTERPRETATION: Square the amplitude's size.
EQUATION: standard error = √(p(1−p)/N)
NAME: Shot-noise (binomial) standard error
MEANING: Typical size of the random error in a measured frequency.
VARIABLES: p = true outcome probability; N = number of shots.
WHY IT MATTERS: Tells learners how many shots they need and how much variation is normal.
BEGINNER INTERPRETATION: More shots help, but only slowly.
EQUATION: Memory (density matrix) ≈ 4ⁿ × 16 bytes
NAME: Density-matrix memory
MEANING: Storing a 2ⁿ × 2ⁿ complex matrix.
VARIABLES: n = number of qubits.
WHY IT MATTERS: Shows why noisy exact simulation reaches fewer qubits than the state-vector method.
BEGINNER INTERPRETATION: Each added qubit multiplies memory by four.
EXAMPLE: n = 15 → 4¹⁵ × 16 bytes = 2³⁰ × 16 = 16 GiB (equivalent to a 30-qubit state vector).
EQUATION: Clifford gates = {H, S, CNOT, …}; Clifford circuits are classically simulable in polynomial time (Gottesman–Knill)
NAME: Gottesman–Knill theorem (informal statement)
MEANING: Circuits that start in computational-basis states, use only Clifford gates and end with computational-basis measurements can be simulated efficiently on a classical computer.
VARIABLES: None.
WHY IT MATTERS: Shows that entanglement alone does not make a circuit hard to simulate.
BEGINNER INTERPRETATION: Some very entangled circuits are still easy for a classical computer.
EXAMPLE: A 40-qubit GHZ circuit (E04).
7. Common Misconceptions
MISCONCEPTION ID: M01
WRONG CLAIM: "A quantum simulator is a (small or weak) quantum computer."
WHY IT SEEMS REASONABLE: The name and the identical-looking results.
WHY IT IS WRONG: A circuit simulator is classical software on a classical computer; nothing quantum happens inside it.
CORRECT STATEMENT: "A quantum circuit simulator is a classical program that calculates what a quantum circuit would do."
EXAMPLE: A laptop simulating 10 qubits is still an ordinary laptop.
TRIGGER WORDS: simulator is a quantum computer, runs on qubits, small quantum computer
MISCONCEPTION ID: M02
WRONG CLAIM: "'Quantum simulator' and 'quantum simulation' mean the same thing."
WHY IT SEEMS REASONABLE: The words are almost identical.
WHY IT IS WRONG: A circuit simulator is software; quantum simulation is the task of modelling quantum systems (molecules, materials); an analog quantum simulator is special quantum hardware.
CORRECT STATEMENT: "The word simulator can refer to classical software, to a physical analog device, or (as 'simulation') to a task; check which is meant."
EXAMPLE: V07.
TRIGGER WORDS: simulator, simulation, analog, same thing
MISCONCEPTION ID: M03
WRONG CLAIM: "A simulator can handle any number of qubits."
WHY IT SEEMS REASONABLE: It is "just software".
WHY IT IS WRONG: A general state needs 2ⁿ amplitudes, so memory and time double with each qubit; ordinary machines top out at around 30–35 qubits for general circuits.
CORRECT STATEMENT: "General state-vector simulation is limited to a few dozen qubits; only special circuit types scale further."
EXAMPLE: E01.
TRIGGER WORDS: unlimited qubits, any number, 100 qubits on my laptop
MISCONCEPTION ID: M04
WRONG CLAIM: "If my circuit works on the simulator, it will give the same results on hardware."
WHY IT SEEMS REASONABLE: It is the same circuit.
WHY IT IS WRONG: Hardware has gate errors, readout errors, decoherence, crosstalk and limited connectivity, and gives finite shots.
CORRECT STATEMENT: "Ideal simulator results are what a perfect machine would give; real hardware results approximate them, with differences caused by noise and constraints."
EXAMPLE: V05; Bell state with small 01/10 counts.
TRIGGER WORDS: same results on hardware, simulator vs real, why 01 and 10 appear
MISCONCEPTION ID: M05
WRONG CLAIM: "Real quantum hardware can show you the full state vector or exact probabilities."
WHY IT SEEMS REASONABLE: Simulators show them.
WHY IT IS WRONG: Hardware returns only sampled measurement outcomes. Recovering the full state requires state tomography, whose cost grows exponentially with qubit number.
CORRECT STATEMENT: "Simulators can display amplitudes and exact probabilities; hardware gives only shot counts."
EXAMPLE: C05.
TRIGGER WORDS: read the state vector from hardware, exact probabilities from device, see the amplitudes
MISCONCEPTION ID: M06
WRONG CLAIM: "Quantum computers can compute things that no classical computer could ever compute."
WHY IT SEEMS REASONABLE: They are described as fundamentally more powerful.

WHY IT IS WRONG: A classical computer can simulate any quantum circuit in principle (as simulators do), just with resources that in general grow exponentially. The difference is efficiency, not what is computable.
CORRECT STATEMENT: "Quantum computers are expected to solve some problems much more efficiently, not to compute functions beyond classical computability."
EXAMPLE: E01; the same circuit can be simulated, but cost doubles per qubit.
TRIGGER WORDS: uncomputable, impossible for classical, beyond Turing
MISCONCEPTION ID: M07
WRONG CLAIM: "Any circuit with entanglement is hard for classical computers to simulate."
WHY IT SEEMS REASONABLE: Entanglement is described as a key quantum resource.
WHY IT IS WRONG: Clifford circuits can produce heavily entangled states (Bell, GHZ) yet are efficiently simulable (Gottesman–Knill); low-entanglement circuits may be simulated with tensor networks.
CORRECT STATEMENT: "Entanglement is not enough for classical hardness; the structure of the circuit matters."
EXAMPLE: E04(c).
TRIGGER WORDS: entangled so hard to simulate, entanglement means advantage
MISCONCEPTION ID: M08
WRONG CLAIM: "A noisy simulator reproduces a real device exactly."
WHY IT SEEMS REASONABLE: It is labelled as modelling noise.
WHY IT IS WRONG: A noise model is an approximation built from measured error rates; real devices have drifting, correlated and hard-to-model errors.
CORRECT STATEMENT: "A noise model gives a plausible, approximate picture of hardware noise, not an exact replica."
EXAMPLE: C06.
TRIGGER WORDS: noisy simulator exact, same noise as hardware, replicates the device
8. Important Definitions
TERM: Quantum computer
DEFINITION: A physical device that performs computation using controlled quantum systems (qubits) and returns classical measurement results.
BEGINNER VERSION: A real machine built from qubits.
RELATED CONCEPTS: C01
TERM: Quantum circuit simulator
DEFINITION: Classical software that computes the effect of a quantum circuit mathematically.
BEGINNER VERSION: A program on a normal computer that works out what a quantum circuit would do.
RELATED CONCEPTS: C02, C03
TERM: State-vector simulator
DEFINITION: A simulator that stores all 2ⁿ amplitudes of an n-qubit pure state and updates them gate by gate.
BEGINNER VERSION: The "list of amplitudes" simulator.
RELATED CONCEPTS: C03
TERM: Density-matrix simulator
DEFINITION: A simulator that stores a 2ⁿ × 2ⁿ matrix, able to represent mixed (noisy) states.
BEGINNER VERSION: A simulator that can handle noise exactly, but only for fewer qubits.
RELATED CONCEPTS: C06, C07
TERM: Stabilizer (Clifford) simulator
DEFINITION: A simulator that efficiently handles circuits made only of Clifford gates with basis-state input and measurement.
BEGINNER VERSION: A fast simulator for a special family of circuits.
RELATED CONCEPTS: C07
TERM: Tensor-network simulator
DEFINITION: A simulator that represents the state as a network of small tensors, efficient when entanglement is limited.
BEGINNER VERSION: A simulator that exploits circuits that are not too entangled.
RELATED CONCEPTS: C07
TERM: Shot
DEFINITION: One execution of a circuit followed by measurement, producing one outcome bit-string.
BEGINNER VERSION: One run of the experiment.
RELATED CONCEPTS: C04
TERM: Noise model
DEFINITION: A mathematical description of errors (gate, readout, decoherence) added to a simulation.
BEGINNER VERSION: A set of rules telling the simulator how to make mistakes like real hardware.
RELATED CONCEPTS: C06
TERM: Decoherence
DEFINITION: Loss of a qubit's quantum behaviour through interaction with its environment.
BEGINNER VERSION: Qubits "forgetting" their quantum state over time.
RELATED CONCEPTS: C06
TERM: Readout error
DEFINITION: An error where the measured value of a qubit differs from its actual state.
BEGINNER VERSION: Misreading a qubit.
RELATED CONCEPTS: C06
TERM: Native gates and connectivity
DEFINITION: The gates a device can execute directly, and which qubit pairs can interact; circuits are compiled to fit them.
BEGINNER VERSION: What the device can actually do in one step, and which qubits can talk to each other.
RELATED CONCEPTS: C01, C06
TERM: Analog quantum simulator
DEFINITION: A controllable physical quantum system built to mimic the behaviour of another quantum system.
BEGINNER VERSION: A special lab quantum system that imitates another one.
RELATED CONCEPTS: C02
TERM: Clifford gates
DEFINITION: A set of gates (including H, S and CNOT) that map certain operators to operators of the same kind; circuits using only them are classically easy to simulate.
BEGINNER VERSION: A special family of gates that classical computers can handle efficiently.
RELATED CONCEPTS: C07
TERM: State tomography
DEFINITION: Reconstructing a quantum state from many measurements on many identical copies.
BEGINNER VERSION: Rebuilding the state from lots of repeated measurements; costly.
RELATED CONCEPTS: C05

ACTIVITY ID: A01
TITLE: Inside the Bell circuit, and which "simulator" is which
OBJECTIVE: See the state vector at each step and separate the three meanings of "simulator".
STARTING STATE: Two qubits in |00⟩, ideal state-vector simulator with "show state vector" enabled.
STEPS:

2. Apply CNOT (control q0, target q1) and read the amplitudes and probabilities.
3. Sort these phrases into the three meanings (V07): "a laptop program running my circuit", "estimating a molecule's energy", "cold atoms in a laser lattice imitating a magnet".
4. Try to find the "show amplitudes" option for a real-device run.

EXPECTED OBSERVATION: After H: amplitudes ≈ (0.707, 0, 0.707, 0) in order 00, 01, 10, 11. After CNOT: (0.707, 0, 0, 0.707); probabilities 0.5 / 0 / 0 / 0.5. Phrase sorting: circuit simulator, quantum simulation (task), analog simulator. No amplitude view exists for hardware.
WHY THIS HAPPENS: The simulator stores the full state; hardware reveals only measurement outcomes.
TRY THIS: Swap the gate order (CNOT first, then H) and compare.
EXPECTED RESULT: CNOT first leaves |00⟩ unchanged; then H gives (|00⟩ + |10⟩)/√2: P(00) = P(10) = 0.5.
OPEN QUESTION: Why can a simulator show amplitudes but a device cannot?
ACTIVITY ID: A02
TITLE: Shots and statistical noise
OBJECTIVE: Observe how counts converge to probabilities.
STARTING STATE: Bell circuit on an ideal simulator in sampling mode.
STEPS:
1. Run with 10, 100, 1,000 and 10,000 shots, three times each.
2. Record the count of 00 each time.
3. Compare the spread with ±√(p(1−p)/N).
EXPECTED OBSERVATION: Counts vary from run to run; spread is wide for 10 shots and narrow for 10,000; 01 and 10 never appear in the ideal simulation.
WHY THIS HAPPENS: Each shot is an independent random sample; relative fluctuations shrink as 1/√N.
TRY THIS: Fix the random seed and repeat to see identical results.
EXPECTED RESULT: Expected fraction of 00 ≈ 0.5 with standard error 0.158 (N=10), 0.05 (N=100), 0.0158 (N=1,000), 0.005 (N=10,000).
OPEN QUESTION: How many shots would you need to halve the error of the N = 1,000 estimate? (Answer direction: about four times as many.)
ACTIVITY ID: A03
TITLE: Ideal vs noisy
OBJECTIVE: See how noise changes a Bell-state result.
STARTING STATE: Bell circuit, 4,000 shots, noise slider at zero.
STEPS:
1. Run on the ideal simulator and note the counts.
2. Switch on a simple noise model (readout error, then gate error) and increase noise gradually.
3. Record when 01 and 10 appear and by how much 00 and 11 fall.
EXPECTED OBSERVATION: With zero noise, 01 and 10 never appear; with noise they appear and grow as the noise level increases.
WHY THIS HAPPENS: Errors move probability into outcomes the ideal circuit forbids.
TRY THIS: Add a longer chain of gates and observe larger deviations.
EXPECTED RESULT: Ideal: 00 ≈ 50%, 11 ≈ 50%, 01 = 10 = 0%. Noisy: 01 and 10 > 0 (exact amounts depend on the chosen model).
OPEN QUESTION: Would you conclude the circuit is wrong if 01 and 10 each appear in about 1–2% of shots? What more would you check?
ACTIVITY ID: A04
TITLE: Where do simulators run out?
OBJECTIVE: Find the practical limits and see how stabilizer simulation escapes them.
STARTING STATE: Memory slider (V03), laptop memory set to 16 GiB.
STEPS:
1. Find the largest n whose state vector fits in 16 GiB.
2. Build GHZ circuits of 5, 10, 20 and 40 qubits (H on q0, then CNOT from each qubit to the next) and run them with a state-vector simulator, then with a stabilizer simulator.
3. Compare run times and which sizes succeed.
EXPECTED OBSERVATION: The state-vector method fails or becomes impractical beyond about 30 qubits on 16 GiB; the stabilizer simulator handles all sizes quickly.
WHY THIS HAPPENS: State-vector memory ∝ 2ⁿ; GHZ circuits are Clifford, so a stabilizer simulator avoids storing 2ⁿ amplitudes.
TRY THIS: Add a single T gate and observe what happens in the stabilizer simulator.
EXPECTED RESULT: Largest n for 16 GiB at 16 bytes/amplitude: 2ⁿ × 16 ≤ 2³⁴ → n ≤ 30. GHZ results (ideal): all-zeros ≈ 50%, all-ones ≈ 50%, all other outcomes 0%.
OPEN QUESTION: If Clifford circuits are easy, which gate would you add to make a circuit hard again?

TYPE: Conceptual
DIFFICULTY: Hard

CORRECT ANSWER: The claim is wrong. The state space grows as 2ⁿ, so 50 qubits have 2⁵⁰/2²⁵ = 2²⁵ = 33,554,432 times more amplitudes than 25 qubits. Equivalently, a general state-vector simulation of 50 qubits would need about 16 PiB rather than 512 MiB. (Separately, a real 50-qubit device is noisy, so its usable computation also depends on error rates; qubit count alone is not "power".)

QUESTION: Why must a quantum-advantage claim be compared with the best classical simulation methods, and why can't a state-vector simulator alone settle the matter?
TYPE: Conceptual
DIFFICULTY: Hard

CORRECT ANSWER: A claim of advantage says no classical method can match the quantum device. State-vector simulation is only one classical method and fails beyond a few dozen qubits, but other methods (tensor networks, stabilizer methods, or clever approximations exploiting structure and noise) can handle special circuits and may reproduce the result, as happened after some earlier claims. So a valid claim must be tested against the best available classical methods, not just against a state-vector simulator.
EXPLANATION: See C07 and Topic 1.3 C08.

17. Topic Summary
What you should now know
A quantum computer is a physical device with real qubits that returns noisy, sampled bit-strings; a quantum circuit simulator is classical software that calculates what a circuit would do.
A state-vector simulator stores 2ⁿ amplitudes (2ⁿ × 16 bytes), applies each gate to them, and can show exact probabilities and full amplitudes — things hardware cannot reveal.
Simulator memory and time double with every extra qubit, so general circuits stop being simulable at around 30–40 qubits on ordinary machines.
Shot counts fluctuate around the true probabilities with standard error √(p(1−p)/N); a 488/512 split of 1000 shots of an ideal 50/50 outcome is normal.
Hardware results differ from ideal simulation because of gate and readout errors, decoherence, crosstalk, limited connectivity and finite shots; noise models approximate but do not replicate this.
Some circuits (Clifford circuits, low-entanglement circuits) are classically easy to simulate even when entangled; this is why advantage claims must be checked against the best classical methods.
"Simulator" can mean classical software, an analog quantum device, or (as "simulation") a task — check which is meant.
